DOI: 10.1002/adma.202205284 wind energy.[1] Rechargeable batteries are important energy storage and conversion devices to coordinate the intermittent electricity generated by renewable energy sources.[2] Lithium–sulfur (Li–S) batteries with a high theoretical energy density (2600 Wh kg−1) are promising next-generation battery systems.[3] Since the breakthrough of the S/carbon composite cathode proposed by Nazar and co-workers in 2009,[4] the development of S cathodes has flourished rapidly.[5] Lithium polysulfide (LiPS) intermediates as inherent redox mediators play a vital role in promoting the conversion kinetics of the S cathode.[6] Under sufficient Li supply (thickness > 500 μm) and regular-loading S cathodes (<2 mg cm−2), Li–S batteries can deliver thousands of cycles.[7] However, when it comes to practical conditions of a limited Li reservoir (thickness < 50 μm) and a low negative to positive capacity ratio (N/P < 2), the continuously parasitic reactions of LiPSs on Li-metal anodes account for the rapid decay of Li-metal anodes and induce limited cycling lifespan of practical Li–S batteries.[8] Various strategies have been proposed to inhibit the parasitic reactions of LiPSs on Li-metal anodes.[9] For example, reducing the concentration of reactants (LiPSs) is a direct approach to suppressing the parasitic reactions of LiPSs, which appeals to numerous researches.[10] Sparingly solvating electrolytes can reduce the solubility of LiPSs from ≈6.0 m to <100 × 10−3 m total S species by reducing the amount of free solvents or introducing a large amount of weak coordination solvents, including “solvent-in-salt” electrolytes,[11] highconcentration electrolytes with diluent,[12] ionic-liquid-based electrolytes,[13] and solvated ionic liquid electrolytes[14] for Li–S batteries.

Nevertheless, the insufficient supply of LiPSs in the sparingly solvating electrolytes induces sluggish sulfur redox reactions and causes Li–S batteries to lose the advantage of high energy density.[15] We proposed a fresh concept of encapsulating-polysulfide electrolytes (EPSE) to inhibit the parasitic reactions of LiPSs on Li-metal anodes and meanwhile maintain satisfactory conversion kinetics of sulfur redox reactions.[16] The inner solvent shell of LiPSs in EPSE is composed of solvents with strong solvating Long cycling lifespan is a prerequisite for practical lithium–sulfur batteries yet is restricted by side reactions between soluble polysulfides and the lithiummetal anode.
The regulation on solvation structure of polysulfides renders encapsulating polysulfides electrolytes (EPSE) as a promising solution to suppress the parasitic reactions.
The solvating power of the solvents in the outer solvent shell of lithium polysulfides is critical for the encapsulation effect of EPSE.
Herein, 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl-2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropyl ether (HFE) is demonstrated as a superior outer-shell solvent to construct EPSE.
Based on the large steric hindrance of the fluorohydrocarbon chains, the electronwithdrawing perfluoro segment (CF2 further endows HFE with prominently weak solvating power.
The HFE-EPSE improves the lifespan from 54 to 135 cycles for lithium–sulfur batteries with an ultrathin lithium-metal anode (50 μm) and high-areal-loading sulfur cathode (4.4 mg cm−2).
Furthermore, a 334 Wh kg−1 lithium–sulfur pouch cell (2.4 Ah level) with HFE-EPSE stably undergoes 25 cycles.

This work demonstrates the role of weakening solvating power of outer-shell solvents to construct superior EPSE and inspires the significance of the solvation chemistry of polysulfides to achieve practical lithium–sulfur batteries.

The introduction of poor solvating power cosolvent renders the formation of EPSE to encapsulate the centered LiPSs and suppress the side reactions in working Li–S batteries.
The reaction kinetics of LiPSs with Li-metal anodes is decreased in EPSE compared with that in routine ether electrolytes even at the same concentration of LiPSs.

According to previous advances, large steric hindrance can effectively weaken the solvating power of molecules[17] and the isopropyl with large steric hindrance makes di-isopropyl sulfide (DIPS) and isopropyl ether (DIPE) to act as effective outer-shell solvents to construct EPSE.[16] However, there is difference in the solvating power between DIPS and DIPE due to the different coordination atoms (S atom in DIPS and O atom in DIPE) and they display different improvement effects on the cycle lifespan of Li–S batteries.[16] Therefore, it is speculated that the solvating power of outer-shell solvents plays a vital role in dictating the effect of EPSE and the underlying mechanism is indistinct.

In order to further improve the electrochemical performance of practical Li–S batteries, EPSE with superior performance is necessary and the design of the outer solvent shell of LiPSs is crucial to encapsulate LiPSs.

Herein, 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl-2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropyl ether (HFE) is demonstrated as a superior outer-shell solvent to construct EPSE to inhibit the side reactions of LiPSs on working Li-metal anodes.
Both the large steric hindrance of fluorohydrocarbon chains and the electron-withdrawing CF2 segments in the HFE molecule ensure the prominently weak solvating power.
HFE only distributes in an outer solvent shell around LiPSs, barely changing the inner solvent shell of LiPSs.
HFE- EPSE dramatically improves the cycling lifespan of Li–S batteries from 54 to 135 cycles with an ultrathin 50 μm Li-metal anode and a high-areal-loading S cathodes of 4.4 mg cm−2.
Moreover, a 2.4 Ah pouch cell with HFE-EPSE undergoes stable 25 cycles with an initial energy density of 334 Wh kg−1. 2.
Results and Discussion 2.1.

Solvation Structure of HFE-EPSE According to previous reports, large steric hindrance enables molecules to possess weak solvating power which can be used as the outer-shell solvents of LiPSs to construct EPSE.[17] Hydrofluoroether not only has large steric hindrance of fluorohydrocarbon chains but also has abundant electron-withdrawing CF segments (such as CF2 and CF3).[18] The electronwithdrawing effect of CF bond is considered to endow hydrofluoroether with extremely low solvating power compared with DIPS and DIPE.
Therefore, hydrofluoroether is expected to have the potential to regulate the LiPS solvation structure, especially as a promising candidate for the outer-shell solvent of LiPSs.
Herein 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl-2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropyl ether (denoted as HFE)[19] is chosen as a representative hydrofluoroether to demonstrate the potential to construct EPSE.
HFE-EPSE consists of 1,3-dioxolane (DOL)/1,2-dimethoxy­ ethane (DME)/HFE (2:2:1, by vol.).

DOL/DME (1:1, by vol.) is used as the typical control solvent due to its wide application in Li–S batteries since the 2000s.[20] Both the electrolytes contain 1.0 m bis-(trifluoromethanesulfonyl) imide (LiTFSI) to provide basic ionic conductivity.[21] The solvation structure of 1.0 m [S] Li2S8, that is the distribution of solvents around LiPSs in DOL/DME or HFE-EPSE, was decoded by molecular dynamics (MD) simulations.

Li+ interacts with S82− tightly both in DOL/DME and HFE-EPSE, implying the dissociation of Li2S8 is weak (Figure 1a,d).[22] In DOL/ DME, DME emerges at 4.4 Å from the center of S82− through S82−–Li+–solvent interactions and the inner solvent shell (shell 1) is formed.
Following DME, DOL appears at 6.6 Å to form the outer solvent shell (shell 2).

The solvation structure of 1.0 m [S] Li2S8 is similar to that in our previous research.[16] The coordination number of Li+, DME, and DOL begins to increase at 2.1, 4.0, and 4.8 Å, respectively, which also reflects the difference in solvating power of the solvents around LiPSs (Figure 1b,c).
The introduction of HFE into DOL/DME dramatically changes the LiPS outer solvent shell other than the inner solvent shell.

Specifically, the inner solvent shell around LiPSs consists of DME (4.4 Å), which is similar to that in DOL/DME to ensure suitable dissolution of LiPSs.[23] HFE emerges at 6.4 Å which is recruited in the second solvent shell (Figure 1d).

The coordination number of Li+, DME, DOL, and HFE around centered S82− begins to increase at 2.1, 4.0, 4.8, and 5.5 Å, respectively, indicating HFE merely influences the structure of the outer solvent shell yet encapsulates centered S82− and the inner solvent shell (Figure 1e,f).
Experiments including nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and Raman spectroscopy were further used to probe the solvation structure of LiPSs.

Considering that solvents interact with LiPSs by S82−–Li+–solvent interactions,[22] 7Li-NMR was used to infer the distribution of solvents around LiPSs. 1.0 m [S] Li2S8 dissolving in DOL/DME or HFE-EPSE is chosen as the electrolyte to imitate the electrolyte formulation used in MD simulations.
The chemical shift of 7Li is 3.20 ppm both for DOL/DME and HFE-EPSE, indicating HFE barely interacts with Li+ and does not change the inner solvent shell of LiPSs (Figure 1g).

Compared with previous research that the introduction of DIPS and DIPE has a little influence of deshielding effect on the chemical shift of 7Li, the decoded solvation structure of HFE-EPSE indicates that the solvating power of HFE is much weaker than DIPS and DIPE, which is beneficial from the large steric hindrance of fluorohydrocarbon chains and electron-withdrawing effect of CF2 segments.
There is a similar conclusion for Raman spectroscopy.

The signal of polysulfides (392, 448, and 510 cm−1), DME (845 cm−1), and DOL (945 cm−1) nearly overlaps for DOL/DME and HFE-EPSE,[24] indicating the inner solvent shell around LiPSs maintains with the introduction of HFE (Figure 1h and Figure S1, Supporting Information).
A similar conclusion is obtained for 1.0 m [S] Li2S6 (Figures S2 and S3, Supporting Information).
Therefore, it is concluded that HFE successfully constructs EPSE (Figure 1i).

In previous researches, the concept of localized high-concentration electrolytes was proposed for Li-ion and Li-metal batteries, where the introduction of hydrofluoroether aims to reduce the apparent concentration of Li salts but enable the electrolyte to exhibit the solvation structure of high-concentration electrolytes.[25] Hydrofluoroether is not involved in the solvation of Li+ due to its poor solvating power.

Inhibited Parasitic Reactions of LiPSs by HFE-EPSE The reduction stability of HFE was investigated through electrochemical tests.
The reduction current begins to increase at 1.2 and 0.9 V of DME and DOL during the cyclic voltammogram (CV) test, respectively (Figure 2a).
The corresponding peak current of DME and DOL is 0.054 and 0.024 mA cm−2, respectively.
In contrast, the reduction current of HFE is only 0.010 mA cm−2, indicating the excellent reduction stability of HFE.

Li–S Batteries with HFE-EPSE under Practical Conditions Specifically, it should be mentioned that the test conditions of Li–S batteries highly influence the evaluation objectivity of the strategies.

Although Li–S batteries can deliver a long lifespan under conventional conditions of regular-loading S cathodes of less than 2 mg cm−2 and enough Li supply with a thickness of more than 500 μm, the mild conditions conceal the problems of Li-metal anodes and exaggerate the effectiveness of anode protection strategies because only low proportion of Li-metal anodes (<4%) is used in each cycle.

Therefore, the practical effect of HFE-EPSE was verified in Li–S batteries under demanding conditions of high-loading S cathodes (4.4 mg cm−2), ultrathin Li anodes (50 μm), and an electrolyte-to-sulfur (E/S) ratio of 6.0 μL mgS−1 with LiNO3 additives (Figure 3a and Figure S4, Supporting Information).
The Li–S batteries were cycled at 0.1 C after initial two cycles of activation at 0.05 C (Figure S5, Supporting Information).
The Li–S battery with DOL/DME electrolyte exhibits an initial specific capacity of 957 mAh g−1 (Figure 3a).
However, the specific capacity sharply decreases after 40 cycles.
The Li–S battery with DOL/ DME only delivers 54 cycles based on 70% capacity retention.
In contrast, the battery with HFE-EPSE undergoes stable 135 cycles based on 70% capacity retention.
The cycling lifespan of the Li–S batteries improves 1.5 times with the employment of HFE-EPSE.
The cycling stability of batteries with HFE-EPSE is superior compared with other advanced electrolyte strategies (Table S1, Supporting Information).

The discharge median voltage of the battery with HFE-EPSE maintains stable above 2.06 V even after 135 cycles, while that with DOL/DME dramatically decreases after 20 cycles and reaches only 2.00 V after 40 cycles (Figure 3b and Figure S6, Supporting Information).
The more stable and higher discharge median voltage enabled by HFE-EPSE indicates the internal resistance of batteries is reduced and the dead Li accumulation is alleviated.

Specifically, the galvanostatic charge and discharge profiles nearly overlap of the Li–S batteries with DOL/DME and HFE-EPSE at the second cycle except for a slight difference in discharge capacity (Figure 3c).
Moreover, the discharge profiles of the Li–S battery with HFE-EPSE maintain stable at the 40th cycle, while that with DOL/DME delivers a dramatical slope of the second discharge plateau.

Furthermore, the rate performance of HFE-EPSE is investigated.

The Li–S batteries with HFE-EPSE deliver specific capacity of 957, 885, 837, 778, and 738 mAh g−1 at 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, and 0.5 C, respectively, indicating that HFE-EPSE can effectively work at different rates (Figure S7, Supporting Information).
Furthermore, a higher-loading S cathode of 6.6 mg cm−2 is used to demonstrate the effect of HFE-EPSE.
The corresponding practical N/P ratio is 1.4, which is much lower than 2.6 of the Li–S batteries with the S cathode of 4.4 mg cm−2.

The lower N/P ratio corresponds to a higher Li utilization ratio (71% vs 38%) and a higher Li utilization amount (7.4 vs 3.9 mAh cm−2), which indicates the parasitic reactions are more severe and can verify the effect of HFE-EPSE.
An initial specific capacity of 1100 mAh g−1 and a capacity retention of 74% after 40 cycles at 0.1 C are achieved in the Li–S battery with HFE-EPSE electrolyte (Figure 3d).
In contrast, an initial specific capacity of 1123 mAh g−1 yet a low capacity retention of 52% after 19 cycles is observed in the Li–S battery with DOL/ DME electrolyte.
The Li–S battery with HFE-EPSE also exhibits a low discharge voltage polarization during cycling (Figure S8, Supporting Information).
HFE-EPSE effectively prolongs the cycle lifespan of Li–S batteries under demanding conditions.
The cycled Li-metal anodes were analyzed to verify the advantages of HFE-EPSE in inhibiting parasitic reactions.

The residual Li in Li–S batteries with DOL/DME is randomly distributed and nonuniform with exposure to the Cu current collector after 40 cycles, while the residual Li is more compact in HFE-EPSE (Figure S9, Supporting Information).
The residual active Li reservoir of the Li-metal anodes in Li–S batteries after 40 cycles was analyzed by a stripping test based on cycled Li|Ni battery configuration.
The residual active Li reservoir of the Li–S battery with HFE-EPSE is 7.3 mAh cm−2, accounting for 73% of the pristine active Li (Figure 4a).
The residual active Li reservoir of the Li–S battery with DOL/DME is 6.1 mAh cm−2, which is less than that of HFE-EPSE.

Practical Li–S Pouch Cells with HFE-EPSE Compared with coin cells, pouch cells can demonstrate the high-energy-density advantage of Li–S batteries from the device scale and provide much demanding conditions to verify the effectiveness of strategies.
A 2.4 Ah-level pouch cell is employed to verify the effect of HFE-EPSE (Figure 5a).
The active materials in electrodes are double-layer and the size of the electrodes is 7 × 4 cm2 (Figure S14, Supporting Information).
High-loading S cathodes (7.2 mg cm−2), ultrathin Li-metal anodes (75 μm), and lean electrolytes (3.5 g gS−1) are used to build a full cell.
The initial discharge energy density is 334 Wh kg−1 (Figure 5b).
After 25 cycles, the pouch cell with HFE-EPSE delivers a high capacity retention of 60% with a relatively stable CE (Figure 5c).

HFE-EPSE is expected to have good compatibility with cathode redox promoters, such as electrochemical catalysis,[30] to improve the conversion kinetics.
Therefore, HFE-EPSE emerges as a promising solution for practical long-cycling and high-energy-density Li–S batteries. 3.
Conclusions HFE is used as a superior outer-shell solvent to construct EPSE to inhibit the intrinsic side reactions between LiPSs and Li-metal anodes.
There are two long fluorohydrocarbon chains with large steric hindrance and abundant electronwithdrawing CF2 segments in the HFE molecule, which enables HFE to have much weak solvating power.
The weak interaction of HFE with LiPSs makes HFE only distribute in the outer solvent shell of LiPSs.
The HFE with high reduction stability ensures the stable preservation of the encapsulation structure during repeated cycling.

HFE-EPSE dramatically improves the cycling life span of Li–S batteries from 54 to 135 cycles based on 70% capacity retention with ultrathin Li-metal anodes (50 μm) and high-loading S cathodes (4.4 mg cm−2).
Moreover, a 2.4 Ah-level Li–S pouch cell with HFE-EPSE delivers stable 25 cycles with an initial energy density of 334 Wh kg–1.
This work demonstrates that HFE is a superior outer-shell solvent to construct EPSE and inspires further effective regulation of solvation structures of LiPSs to achieve long-cycling Li–S batteries.

Raw materials Li metal foils (China Energy Lithium Co., Ltd.), 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME, battery grade, DoDoChem), 1,3-dixolane (DOL, battery grade, DoDoChem), lithium bis-(trifluoromethanesulfonyl) imide (LiTFSI, battery grade, DoDoChem), N-methyl- 2-pyrrolidinone (NMP, Sinopharm), poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF, HSV-300), sulfur (S), multi-walled carbon nanotubes (CNTs), aluminum (Al) foil, and lithium nitrate (LiNO3, metals basis, Aladdin) were used as purchased without purification. 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl-2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropyl ether (HFE, 98%, TCI) was purified by molecular sieve for 24 h. 2.
The preparation of sulfur cathode S powder and CNTs (7:3 by wt.) were mixed to form S/CNT composite.
Then, the S/CNT composite and PVDF binder (9:1, by wt.) were ball-milled in NMP.
The obtained slurry was cast onto Al foil and further dried at 60°C for 12 h.
The S/C cathode was cut into disks (Φ13.0 mm) with a S content of 63%.
The S loading is 1.3, 4.4, and 6.6 mg cm−2 for coin cells.
The S cathode was kept in an argon-filled glove box with O2 and H2O contents below 0.1 ppm. 3.
The preparation of electrolytes The control electrolyte was composed of 1.0 M LiTFSI in DOL/DME (1:1, by vol.) and was denoted as DOL/DME.
The electrolyte composed of 1.0 M LiTFSI in DOL/DME/HFE (2:2:1, by vol.) was denoted as HFE-EPSE.
LiNO3 was employed in the electrolytes to improve the performance of the Li–S coin cells with high-loading S
SI2 cathodes and ultrathin Li metal anodes.
Li2S and S (1:7, by mol.) were added into the DOL/DME or HFE-EPSE electrolyte to prepare the Li2S8 electrolyte.
Li2S and S (1:5, by mol.) were added into the DOL/DME or HFE-EPSE electrolyte to prepare the Li2S6 electrolyte.
All electrolytes were prepared in an argon-filled glove box with O2 and H2O contents below 0.1 ppm. 4.
Electrochemical measurements Li–S batteries were assembled in standard 2032-coin cells with polypropylene (PP) separators (Celgard 2400).
Li–S batteries under mild conditions were assembled with a Li metal anode (600 μm), a regular-loading S cathode (1.3 mg cm−2), and 25 μL electrolyte without LiNO3.

Li–S batteries under demanding conditions were assembled with an ultrathin Li anode (50 μm), a high-loading S cathode (4.4 or 6.6 mg cm−2), and electrolyte (35 or 60 μL, respectively) containing 2.0 wt.% LiNO3.
The cells were tested between 1.7–2.6 V at different C-rates (1 C = 1672 mA g−1) on a Neware battery cycler (CT-4008t, Shenzhen, China).

For the shuttle current test, Li–S batteries under mild conditions without LiNO3 were galvanostatically charged to 2.9 V and then discharged potentiostaticlly to 2.90, 2.60, 2.45, 2.43, 2.40, 2.39, 2.38, 2.37, 2.36, 2.35, 2.34, 2.25, and 2.20 V step by step.
The shuttle current was determined by the steady-state current at different potentiostatic voltages. 5.
Material Characterizations The morphologies of Li metal anodes were observed by a scanning electron microscope (SEM, JSM 7401F, JEOL Ltd., Japan) operated at 3.0 kV.

SI3 from Li–S batteries were washed three times by DME to remove residual electrolyte and dried in the glove box. 7Li nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra (JNM- ECA600) were recorded at 233.2 MHz at room temperature.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) were conducted on scanning X-ray microprobe (Axis Supra+, Kratos Analytical) operated at 250 kV with monochromated Al Kα radiation.
The Ar+ sputtering rate was ~130 nm min–1 calibrated on Ta2O5 surface. 6.
Li–S pouch cells Li–S pouch cells were fabricated in a dry room (dew point < −40°C).
The size of electrodes was 7 × 4 cm2.
The S loading was 7.2 mg cm−2 for each side with S content of 63% (by weight).
The thickness of ultrathin Li foils was 75 μm for each single side.
The electrolyte/sulfur (E/S) ratio was 3.5 g gS−1.
The Li–S pouch cells were cycled at 1.8–2.5 V and 0.05 C (1 C = 1000 mA g−1).

The energy density was evaluated as follws: E = Ed/(mLi + mS + mCu + mAl + msep + mtap + mely + mpack) where E is the gravimetric energy density, Ed is the initial discharge energy, mLi, mS, mCu, mAl, msep, mtap, mely, and mpack stand for the mass of Li metal anodes, S cathodes (S, carbon, and binder), Cu current collector, Al current collector, separator, tap, electrolyte, and package, respectively.
The pouch cells with HFE-EPSE delivered an initial discharge energy of 5.04 Wh.
The total mass of the battery core (Li metal anodes, S cathodes, Cu current collector, Al current collector, separator, and tap) was 5.88 g.
The mass of electrolyte and package were 7.12 and 2.10 g, respectively.
The initial energy density based on the total mass of the pouch cell was 334 Wh kg−1. 7.

SI4 MD simulations were performed based on the LAMMPS code[1] and OPLS-AA force field.[2] The force field parameters were generated by the LigParGen web server[3] except that restrained electrostatic potential (RESP) atomic partial charges were assigned to each atom, which was obtained based on electrostatic potential (ESP) charges using the Multiwfn program.[4] The parameters for Li+, TFSI−, and S82− were obtained from Jensen et al.,[5] Koddermann et al.,[6] and Rajput et al.,[7] respectively.
Two models with and without HFE were constructed.
The model with HFE contains 458 DOL, 308 DME, 80 LiTFSI, 10 Li2S8, and 105 HFE molecules while the one without HFE contains 572 DOL, 385 DME, 80 LiTFSI, and 10 Li2S8 molecules.
The initial atomic coordinates were generated with Packmol[8] program and the final constructions were visualized by VESTA[9] and VMD.[10] The time step was fixed to be 1 fs for all simulations.

All systems were first equilibrated in NPT ensemble using the Parrinello–Rahman barostat[11] for 2 ns to maintain a temperature of 298 K and a pressure of 1 atm with time constants of 0.1 and 1 ps, respectively.

Subsequently, the models were heated from 298 to 420 K for 2 ns and maintained at 420 K for 4 ns, followed by annealing from 420 to 298 K in 2 ns and equilibrated at 298 K in NPT ensemble for another 4 ns.
A production run of 12 ns at 298 K in NVT ensemble under Nose–Hoover thermostat[12] was finally conducted.
The last 5 ns NVT simulations were used for the solvation structure analyses.
